For reference, we'll talk about an aqueous solution of nickel (II) chloride poured over solid aluminum.

WHAT THE HECK IS GOING ON?

Well, there are only two compounds here - one's a metal and one's a salt. Even if we know nothing about chemistry, the AB + C -> A + CB format for ion exchange is pretty standard. You can assume that most problems thrown at you will be straightforward like this, because the teacher would rather see you demonstrate skill in setting up redox reactions than pick apart the ambiguity of multiple equilibrium points.

A solid metal is already at its most reduced state, so that gives us only one direction for aluminum to go: oxidation. Since we know this is a test on redox reactions and we've eliminated all but one reaction, this is pretty well locked down. Even if we didn't have that narrowed down, you should know that aluminum has a high electronegativity and is likely to steal the oxidation state from nickel.

Get a feeling for which metals are more likely to steal from each other - the electronegativity scale isn't a perfect reference, for example in this reaction nickel is actually more likely to take electrons than aluminum, but in that case there'd be no reaction and it's doubtful the teacher would give you a trick question. Oxygen is more common than fluorine, and they both steal electrons from just about everyone. Remember your polyatomic ions, and refer to periodic trends when comparing metals.

In conclusion, we used a little logic to narrow down our options and referred to electronegativity as well as the commonly known properties of individual elements to decide that this is our overall reaction:

NiCl + Al ---> AlCl + Ni(s)

Nickel's oxidation state is given, and chlorine can only take one electron. Now what oxidation state does aluminum want? Spoilers: Al(III) is the most stable. That gives us enough information to balance our reaction:

3(NiCl2) + 2 Al ---> 2(AlCl3) + 3 Ni

That's already looking pretty good!

OXIDATION/REDUCTION HALF REACTIONS

Now we need to look at each individual element and watch what happens to it. Put a mental camera fixed on each atom as the reaction progresses: where does it begin and where does it end?

Nickel starts out in the (+2) oxidation state and ends up at (0) oxidation as a metal precipitate. It gets reduced.

Chlorine starts out in the (-1) oxidation state and ends in the same place. No change.

Aluminum starts out in the (0) metallic state and ends up bonded to chlorine in the (+3) state. It's been oxidized.

Now let's write out those statements in chemical terms instead of sentences:

Ni(+2) + 2 e- ---> Ni(0)

Cl(-1) ---> Cl(-1)

Al(0) ---> Al(-3) + 3 e-

Those three partial reactions should combine to make the whole overall reaction as a way to double-check your work.
